/journal/the-case-for-a-slower-launch.title: Why a soft launch beats a big launch day
/journal/the-case-for-a-slower-launch.description: Open quietly to fifty friendly customers first. What usually breaks in week one, how to run a soft launch and when to hold the big day.
h2: The case for a slower launch
What goes wrong in week one
Quiet first or straight to loud?
h3: “We opened booking to fifty members first. They found the bugs, and then they told everyone else.”
Why your logo doesn’t need to explain everything
Our favourite Framer tricks for small business sites
Packaging people keep on the shelf
p: Why we sometimes suggest launching quietly first, and how a soft opening can make the big day a lot less scary.
Everyone pictures launch day the same way: a countdown, a queue around the corner and a cork hitting the ceiling.
What we usually see instead is a typo in the headline, a contact form that emails nobody and a founder refreshing their inbox at midnight. There is a calmer way to do it.
A soft launch means opening the doors quietly, to a small group, a week or two before you tell the world. The site is live, the shop is taking orders, and only your friendliest customers know.
Tom Okafor, marketing lead at Moonlit Swim Club
Something always does. After more than 60 launches, we can nearly predict the list:
A link that points at the old website.
A photo that looked fine on a laptop and enormous on a phone.
A payment step nobody tested with a real card.
An opening time that changed last month.
None of these is a disaster when fifty kind people spot it. Each one stings when five thousand strangers do.
Our soft launches follow the same three beats, whatever the size of the business.
Invite the people who already like you. Send them a personal note, not a newsletter, and tell them they’re seeing it first.
Keep it to two questions: “Did anything confuse you?” and “What did you look for and not find?” You’ll learn more from those than from any survey.
Mend what they found. Resist adding new ideas; this fortnight is for repairs, not renovations.
Now send the announcement, pop the cork and enjoy it. The queue can form, because you already know the doors open properly.
Here is how the two approaches compare.
Launching slowly doesn’t mean launching sadly. The big day arrives a fortnight later, and you get to enjoy it instead of firefighting.

/journal/naming-your-business-without-lo.title: How to name your business: a simple method
/journal/naming-your-business-without-lo.description: Start with a feeling, learn the four kinds of name, build a shortlist in four steps and test the finalists before you register anything.
h2: Naming your business without losing your mind
Start with a feeling, not a word
Know the four kinds of name
Pick one and get on with it
h3: “We had 140 names on the wall. The right one was number three. We needed the other 137 to be sure.”
Why your logo doesn’t need to explain everything
Our favourite Framer tricks for small business sites
Packaging people keep on the shelf
h4: When the web address is taken
p: A friendly, step-by-step way to find a name you’ll still like in ten years, even if every good domain seems taken.
Naming a business is like naming a baby, except the baby also needs a web address and nobody’s grandmother gets a vote.
It is the job founders dread most, and we have sat through enough naming sessions to know why. The good news: there is a method, and it mostly involves writing down terrible ideas.
Before you open a thesaurus, decide how people should feel when they say the name out loud. Cosy? Clever? Slightly mischievous? Write that down first and pin it up.
Every name you consider later gets held against that note. It saves hours of arguing about words that were never right for you.
Nearly every business name falls into one of four families. Knowing which one suits you cuts the search in half.
Set aside one afternoon, a big sheet of paper and a friend who will be honest with you.
Fill the page with at least fifty names, bad ones included.
Cross out anything that fights the feeling on your note.
Circle the five you’d be happy to say on the phone.
Sleep on them, then put those five through the tests below.
Fifty sounds like a lot. It isn’t, and the dreadful ones are what shake the good ones loose.
Jonah Reid, owner of Fieldnotes Records
A name that looks handsome on paper can still trip up in the real world. Two quick checks catch most problems.
Ring a friend and tell them the name once, without spelling it. If they can write it down correctly, you’re safe. If they ask “is that with a K?”, think again.
Picture the name on a van in a decade. “Dave’s Laptop Repairs” is awkward once Dave starts selling phones. Leave yourself room to grow.
Don’t panic, and don’t add a hyphen. Putting “hello”, “studio” or your town in front works nicely, and nobody minds.
No name feels perfect on day one. It earns its meaning from the work you do under it, the same way a logo does.
So choose the finalist that makes you smile, register it this week and move on to the fun part. Stuck between two? Say hello and we’ll happily cast the deciding vote.

/journal/what-a-brand-sprint-actually-lo.title: What happens in a two-day brand sprint
/journal/what-a-brand-sprint-actually-lo.description: An hour-by-hour look at a two-day brand sprint: the wall of sticky notes, the one sentence, three rough directions and what you leave with.
h2: What a brand sprint actually looks like
Is a sprint right for you?
h3: “By Tuesday lunchtime we had words for the feeling we’d been failing to describe for a year.”
Why your logo doesn’t need to explain everything
Our favourite Framer tricks for small business sites
Packaging people keep on the shelf
p: Two days, one big wall, a lot of sticky notes and exactly the right number of biscuits. A peek behind the curtain.
A brand sprint sounds athletic. In practice it is eight people, one long wall and a worrying quantity of sticky notes.
We run them in our Hackney studio over two days, and clients often arrive unsure what they have signed up for. So here is the whole thing, hour by hour.
Let’s start at the end, because that is what you’re paying for. By the second afternoon you walk out holding:
One sentence that says who you’re for and why you’re different.
A logo direction everybody in the room has agreed on.
A palette and a pair of typefaces to go with it.
A short list of what happens next, and who does it.
It isn’t a finished identity. Think of it as the foundations poured and the walls marked out in chalk.
Nobody opens a laptop before lunch. The first day is for finding out what is true about your business, which is rarely what is written on the website.
We cover the wall with three columns: what your customers love, what annoys them and what nobody else in your world is doing. Everyone writes. Nobody edits.
Then the pruning starts. We group the notes, argue kindly and boil the lot down to a single line. It usually takes four attempts and one walk around the block.
One packet per four people, per half day. Biscuit the studio dog gets none, however hard he stares.
With the sentence pinned up where we can see it, the designers take over.
The rough directions really are rough: marker pen, not pixels. It keeps everyone talking about the idea instead of the kerning.
Maya Chen, founder of Studio Stretch
Sprints suit businesses that need to move and can get their decision-makers in one room. They’re a poor fit if the person with the final say can only “pop in at four”.
Not sure which camp you’re in? Book a 30 minute call and we’ll tell you honestly. We’ll even supply the biscuits.

/journal/packaging-people-keep-on-the-sh.title: Packaging design people keep on the shelf
/journal/packaging-people-keep-on-the-sh.description: Good packaging gets a second life as a pencil pot or a button box. The three qualities keepers share, and a test to run before you print.
h2: Packaging people keep on the shelf
Before you send anything to print
h3: “Our takeaway tins come back as plant pots on the windowsill. Best free advertising we’ve ever had.”
Why your logo doesn’t need to explain everything
Our favourite Framer tricks for small business sites
What a brand sprint actually looks like
p: The secret to packaging that never makes it to the recycling bin, plus a few boxes we’re still secretly proud of.
Good packaging gets used twice: once to sell the thing, and again as a pencil pot, a plant pot or a treasured shoebox.
That second life is the best advertising you will never pay for. Your name sits on a kitchen shelf for years, long after the coffee has been drunk.
Before we draw anything, we ask one question: what will this box be doing in six months? If the honest answer is “landfill”, we start again.
Here are a few second careers we have seen with our own eyes.
Look along anybody’s shelf of saved packaging and the same three qualities turn up.
Nobody keeps a box that collapses when the cat sits on it. Thicker board, a proper lid and corners that survive the journey home all earn their place.
A tin with a tight lid, a jar with a wide mouth, a bag with long handles. The container should be good at a job beyond holding your product.
Pattern inside the lid. A joke on the base. One colour printed beautifully beats four printed badly.
Sturdier stock does cost more per unit. Set that against free shelf space in a customer’s home, and the sums usually come out smiling.
Sam Rivera, co-owner of Paper Kite Cafe

Tiny Giants Coffee roast micro-lots from small farms, and their old bags looked like everyone else’s on a crowded shelf. We switched to sturdy kraft, gave each farm its own tiny giant character and printed the roast number large enough to read at 7am.
The part we’re quietly proud of is what happened next. Regulars started collecting the characters, and the empty bags now hold everything from teabags to clothes pegs.
Hold the mock-up in your hands and be strict with yourself:
Would you keep it if it arrived at your own door?
Does it still look good once the label is peeled off?
Can it be refilled, reused or handed on?
Two yeses and you’re close. Three, and you have packaging that will outlast the product inside it. If you’d like a second pair of eyes first, book a 30 minute call.

/journal/our-favourite-framer-tricks-for.title: Framer tricks for small business websites
/journal/our-favourite-framer-tricks-for.description: Five habits that keep a small business website easy to update: use the CMS, keep motion gentle, build with styles and picture the phone first.
h2: Our favourite Framer tricks for small business sites
Put anything that changes in the CMS
h3: “I change the plant of the week from my phone, usually in the queue at the garden centre.”
Why your logo doesn’t need to explain everything
Packaging people keep on the shelf
What a brand sprint actually looks like
p: Five little things that make a Framer site feel hand-made, from CMS-powered menus to scroll effects that don’t make anyone seasick.
Most small business websites get built once and then quietly gather dust. The owner is too nervous to touch anything in case the whole page falls over.
We build in Framer because it cures that fear. These are the five habits that make our sites feel hand-made on launch day and still tidy two years later.
Our rule of thumb: if it changes more than twice a year, it belongs in the CMS. Updating a menu then means filling in a form, with no layout to break.
Once that split is made, owners stop being scared of their own website.
Lena Voss, owner of Hello Plant Co.
One lovely moment beats twenty twitchy ones. Each page gets a single piece of movement worth noticing, and everything else sits still.
Opening and closing. Menus, questions, anything that hides and shows.
One arrival. A headline that types itself in, once.
A reply. A button that reacts when someone taps it.
Hijacked scrolling, parallax on every photo and paragraphs that fade in a line at a time. Your visitors came for the opening hours, not a fairground ride.
Flick through the page quickly on your phone. If your stomach notices, take half the effects out.
Every colour and text size on our sites comes from a shared style. Change the blue once and it updates on each page, button and footer link.
Components work the same way. We design one button and reuse it forty times, so a tweak on Monday doesn’t turn into a treasure hunt on Tuesday.
Most visits to a café or shop site come from somebody standing on the pavement, wondering if you’re open. So we sketch the small screen before the big one and check three things:
The hours and address sit near the top.
Every button is big enough for a thumb.
The text reads comfortably without pinching.
Our last trick isn’t in Framer at all. Every site we hand over comes with a one-page guide: where to change the hours, how to add a post and who to ring when something looks odd.
It takes us an hour to write, and it means the website keeps getting used. Want one built this way? Say hello and tell us what yours needs to do.

/journal/why-your-logo-doesnt-need-to-ex.title: Why your logo shouldn’t explain everything
/journal/why-your-logo-doesnt-need-to-ex.description: A logo is a name tag, not a résumé. See what a logo is for, how to spot a kitchen-sink logo, and how one bakery found its single idea.
h2: Why your logo doesn’t need to explain everything
What a logo is actually for
How Good Crumb found its one idea
Let the rest of the brand talk
h3: The jobs to hand to someone else
“I wanted the whole bakery in the logo. I’m so glad they talked me out of it.”
Our favourite Framer tricks for small business sites
Packaging people keep on the shelf
What a brand sprint actually looks like
p: The best logos are a little mysterious. Here’s why we talk clients out of cramming the whole business into one tiny mark.
A logo is a name tag, not a résumé. It has to be recognisable at a glance on a coffee cup, a van and a phone screen, which is a lot to ask of one small shape.
Yet most briefs we receive ask for a mark that shows the product, the values, the founding year and, ideally, the founder’s dog. We love dogs. Ours is called Biscuit. He is still not in our logo.
A logo has one job: helping people spot you again. Everything else it gets credit for is borrowed from the experiences around it.
Think of the swoosh or the bitten apple. Neither explains shoes or computers. They became meaningful because millions of good moments were attached to them afterwards.
Strip away the wish list and three duties remain.
Be recognised. Across a street, in a feed, at thumbnail size.
Be remembered. One idea sticks; five slide off.
Be flexible. It should survive embroidery, a rubber stamp and a favicon.
Telling your story belongs to your website. Proving your quality belongs to your product. Showing your personality belongs to your tone of voice, your photography and the way you answer the phone.
When a mark tries to say everything, it ends up saying nothing clearly. We call it the kitchen-sink logo, and most high streets have at least one.
The symptoms are easy to read: a wheat sheaf, a rolling pin, a sunrise and a banner, all squeezed into a circle the size of a 10p coin.
Shrink yours to the size of a fingernail. If you can still tell what it is, you’re in good shape. If it turns into a smudge, something needs to go.

Good Crumb Bakery came to us wanting loaves, wheat, an oven and a smiling baker. Instead, we spent a morning behind the counter and noticed every customer asking for the same thing: the end of the loaf, the crusty bit.
So the identity became a chunky, slightly wonky wordmark that looks hand-stamped onto a flour sack. No wheat. No oven. The bags, the aprons and one very famous tote carry the rest.
Priya Shah, founder of Good Crumb Bakery
Your logo is the handshake; the conversation happens elsewhere. Before adding another detail to the mark, ask where that detail could live instead:
Could a line of copy say it?
Nine times out of ten the answer is yes, and the symbol gets to stay simple. If yours is carrying too much luggage, book a 30 minute call and we’ll help it travel lighter.

/journal/how-to-give-feedback-your-desig.title: How to give useful design feedback
/journal/how-to-give-feedback-your-desig.description: Say how a design makes you feel before saying what to change. Four habits and a short template for feedback your designer can act on.
h2: How to give feedback your designer can use
Say what you feel before what you’d change
Three habits of our favourite clients
h3: “The best note I ever passed on was a single line: “It looks expensive, and we’re not.” The designers fixed it in an afternoon.”
Why your logo doesn’t need to explain everything
Our favourite Framer tricks for small business sites
Packaging people keep on the shelf
h4: When you really can’t explain it
p: “Make it pop” helps nobody. Four simple habits that turn vague reactions into notes a designer can act on the same day.
“Can you make it pop?” is the most common note a designer receives. It’s also the least useful, and we say that with love.
Good feedback is a skill nobody teaches clients. It takes five minutes to learn, and it will save you a round of revisions.
Your reaction is gold. Your fix might not be. “This feels too serious for us” tells us everything. “Make the logo bigger” only tells us one thing to try.
It feels quiet next to our rivals
Green reminds me of our old brand
None of these feels friendly yet
After more than 60 launches, the projects that ran smoothly had these in common.
One list, from one person, on one day. Comments arriving in eleven separate messages is how details go missing.
Every project starts with an agreed aim. The best notes test the work against it: “Will this make a first-time visitor book?”
First reactions are loud and often wrong. A night’s rest turns “I hate it” into “the colour is fine, the heading is the problem”.
Send us something you do like and say why. A photo of a shop front or a cereal box is a perfectly good brief.
Ruth Clarke, studio manager at Sunday Studio
Next time a design lands in your inbox, answer these in order:
What was your first reaction, in a word or two?
What is working and should stay?
What feels wrong, and what does it remind you of?
Is anything missing that the project needs?
Four answers, one email, and we can get straight to work. Got a project that needs a fresh pair of eyes? Book a 30 minute call.

/journal/lovely-packaging-on-a-small-bud.title: Packaging ideas for a small budget
/journal/lovely-packaging-on-a-small-bud.description: No budget for custom boxes? A rubber stamp, a sticker and a paper belly band can brand stock packaging for pennies per order.
h2: Lovely packaging on a small budget
Start with stock, then make it yours
Three tools that do most of the work
How Hello Plant Co. ships a fern
h3: “We spent more on the stamp than on the first hundred boxes. Two years on, we’re still using the same stamp.”
Why your logo doesn’t need to explain everything
Our favourite Framer tricks for small business sites
Packaging people keep on the shelf
p: Custom boxes need big orders. A rubber stamp, a roll of stickers and a paper band can do the same job for pennies.
Custom boxes are wonderful. They are also sold in minimum orders of five thousand, which is awkward when you sell forty candles a month.
Plenty of our favourite packaging cost almost nothing to make. It works because somebody chose one good idea and repeated it.
Buy the plainest carton, bag or jar your supplier already carries. Then add a single layer that belongs to you.
You can build an entire system from this short shopping list.
Your logo in one colour of ink, on anything that stays still. Slightly uneven prints look hand-made, because they are.
One size, one design, used to seal tissue, close bags and label jars.
A strip of printed paper wrapped round a plain box. It turns a stock carton into a product for the price of a sheet of A4.
Never economise on whatever protects the product. A beautiful stamp on a crushed parcel is still a crushed parcel.
Hello Plant Co. post living plants, which is hard on cardboard and on nerves. Their parcels are plain, stock-size cartons with a green stamp on the lid and a care card tucked in the soil.
The only printed extra is a belly band reading “This way up. I’m alive in here.” Couriers, it turns out, are gentler with boxes that talk.
Lena Voss, owner of Hello Plant Co.
Stock and stamps aren’t a compromise; they’re a stage. You’ll know it’s time for a printed box when:
You reorder the same carton every single month.
Stamping has started to slow down the packing table.
Customers recognise your parcel before they read the label.
Until then, keep to a single ink, a single sticker and a single idea. Need help choosing the idea? Say hello.

/journal/what-a-good-unboxing-feels-like.description: Plan an unboxing in three beats: the outside, the reveal and the product. Where to spend the packaging budget and how to rehearse it.
h2: What a good unboxing feels like
How Good Crumb boxes a birthday cake
h3: “Someone sent us a video of their gran opening the box. She gasped at the lid, before she had even seen the cake.”
Why your logo doesn’t need to explain everything
Our favourite Framer tricks for small business sites
Packaging people keep on the shelf
p: The best ten seconds of buying online happen before the product appears. How to plan the outside, the reveal and the keepsake.
The best ten seconds of buying something online happen before you see the product. It’s the moment the lid comes off.
Shops have music, smells and a person who says hello. A parcel has cardboard. Here is how to make cardboard do all three jobs.
We plan every box like a very short play.
The shipping carton should be plain, sturdy and clearly yours. One stamp or a strip of printed tape is plenty. Save the fireworks.
This is the lift of the lid. Tissue, a printed inner flap or a change of colour gives the hands something to do and the eyes something new.
Finally the product, sitting snugly, facing up and looking expected. Nothing should rattle.
A handwritten-style note, a sticker or a recipe card costs pennies. It’s also the part people photograph.
You can’t afford to make every surface special, and you shouldn’t try.

Good Crumb Bakery sends celebration cakes across the city in a plain kraft carrier. Open it and the inside is printed in the bakery’s checked pattern, with a card that reads “Candles are in the side pocket. You’re welcome.”
Customers keep that card. Several have it stuck to the fridge.
Priya Shah, founder of Good Crumb Bakery
Before you commit to a thousand cartons, pack one and hand it to a friend who hasn’t seen it. Watch closely and keep quiet.
Do they know which way up it goes?
Do they pause and smile at any point?
Their face will tell you more than any mock-up on a screen. When you’re ready to design the real thing, book a 30 minute call.

/journal/your-about-page-is-not-about-yo.title: How to write an About page people trust
/journal/your-about-page-is-not-about-yo.description: An About page helps visitors decide whether to trust you. Lead with who you help, prove it briefly, use real photos and end with a way in.
h2: Your About page is not about you
h3: “Our old About page was four hundred words on our process. The new one has a photo of the dog. Enquiries went up.”
Why your logo doesn’t need to explain everything
Our favourite Framer tricks for small business sites
Packaging people keep on the shelf
p: Nobody reads an About page to learn about you. They read it to decide whether to trust you. Here’s how to help them.
Here is an awkward truth about About pages. Nobody opens one to learn about you.
They open it to decide whether they can trust you with their money, their project or their Saturday. Every line should help them make that call.
An About page is a job interview where you can’t see the interviewer. Behind the politeness, the questions are blunt.
Will I like working with them?
What happens if I get in touch?
Picture a single person reading. Ours is a bakery owner with flour on her phone, scrolling between batches.
Open with who you help and how. “We make brands for small, stubborn businesses” beats “Founded in 2017” every time.
Now the history earns its place. Ours fits in a breath: seven people and a dog in Hackney, four-day weeks since 2023, more than 60 launches.
Use real ones, even slightly wonky. A blurred picture of your actual team will win more trust than a perfect image of strangers in a meeting room.
Most of these pages improve by subtraction. Look for the following and cut them:
Any sentence starting with “We are passionate about”.
A timeline with more than five dates.
Awards nobody outside your industry has heard of.
What’s left will be shorter and far more convincing.
Tom Reeve, co-founder of Sunday Studio
The last thing a reader sees should be a way in: a button, an email address or a phone number, with a line saying what happens next.
Ours says we reply within a day, because we do. If yours needs a rewrite, say hello and tell us who it’s for.

/journal/what-to-put-on-your-homepage.title: What to put on your homepage
/journal/what-to-put-on-your-homepage.description: Visitors ask three questions in the first five seconds. What a small business homepage should keep, what to cut, and a quick test for yours.
h2: What to put on your homepage, and what to leave off
The three questions every visitor asks
h3: “People used to ring us to ask how to book. Now they just book.”
Why your logo doesn’t need to explain everything
Our favourite Framer tricks for small business sites
Packaging people keep on the shelf
p: A homepage has five seconds to answer three questions. What to keep, what to cut and a quick test to run on yours.
A homepage has about five seconds to answer one question: am I in the right place?
Most don’t. They open with a slideshow, a mission statement and a photograph of a handshake, and the visitor leaves none the wiser.
Forget clever structure for a moment. People arriving on your site want to know:
What is this? Say it in plain words, above everything else.
Is it for me? Show who you work with or what it costs.
What do I do next? Give them one obvious button.
Answer those in that order and you’re ahead of most of the internet.
Space at the top of a site is like space in a shop window. Whatever you put there says “this matters most”.
Your one-line description, your best piece of work, a real photograph and a way to get in touch. Opening hours too, if you have a door.
Anything written to impress the people who already work for you.
If you wouldn’t tape it to the glass of a real shop, it doesn’t belong above the fold.
Moonlit Swim Club could have led with the restored lido, the lanterns or the DJ. Members only ever wanted one thing from the site, though: a lane, tonight.
So the page opens with the next three swims and a button marked “Book a lane”. The atmosphere lives further down for anybody who wants to linger.
Tom Okafor, marketing lead at Moonlit Swim Club
Show your homepage to someone who has never seen it, count to five and close the laptop. Then ask what you do.

/journal/how-many-colours-does-a-brand-r.title: How many colours does a brand need?
/journal/how-many-colours-does-a-brand-r.description: Most small businesses need three brand colours: one to be recognised by, one for text and one background. How to pick yours in an afternoon.
h2: How many colours does a brand really need?
How Fern & Fable ended up with three
h3: “The hardest part of choosing colours is leaving good ones out. It gets easier after the first three.”
Why your logo doesn’t need to explain everything
Our favourite Framer tricks for small business sites
Packaging people keep on the shelf
p: Most small brands need three colours, not nine. Here’s how to choose them, when to add more and a squint test that settles arguments.
Open a tin of 120 colouring pencils and most of us reach for the same six. Brands work the same way, however long the palette in the guidelines.
We’ve built identities with two colours and identities with nine. The ones that last tend to sit at the small end, and here is why.
Three shades will carry almost any small business: one to be recognised by, one to write in and one to rest on.
Everything else is decoration, and decoration is where budgets and consistency go to die.
Rules are there to be bent, carefully. A few businesses do need a longer list.
A coffee roaster with eight farms or a bakery with a seasonal menu can give each product its own hue, provided the logo and the type never change.
Bright and plentiful suits the audience. Even then, pick a leader and let the others follow.
Pin your packaging to a wall, step back and squint. If you can still tell it’s yours, the palette works. If it turns into confetti, remove one and squint again.

Fern & Fable Books arrived with a mood board of fourteen shades, all lovely. We spent an afternoon in the shop and noticed the bottle green of the old door, the cream of the pages and a red ribbon the sisters tie round every purchase.
That was the palette. It was already there, and customers already knew it.
Mira Hale, co-founder of Sunday Studio
You don’t need a designer to make a start:
Write down the single colour people already link with you.
Choose a dark shade of it, or a plain ink, for text.
Add one quiet background: off-white, grey or cream.
Use only those three for a month and see what you miss.
If the answer is “nothing”, you’re done. If you miss something badly, say hello and we’ll help you find a fourth that earns its place.

/projects/the-yard-workspace.title: The Yard Workspace signage and wayfinding
/projects/the-yard-workspace.description: A letter-and-word wayfinding system for a co-working space in an old print works, from room signs to sandwich boards.
h2: Nobody should end up in the boiler room
h3: “New members stopped knocking on the boiler room door looking for the café. That alone was worth it.”
p: Signs and wayfinding for a co-working space in an old print works, where every corridor looked the same.
We gave every room a letter and a word, set them big on black, and carried the same system out onto the street with sandwich boards and a hanging sign.
The Yard moved into an old print works and kept its brick walls, steel stairs and long corridors. The building was beautiful. It was also very easy to get lost in.
Rooms went by nicknames only the founders understood, and the signs were office paper taped to doors.
We walked the building with new members and wrote down every wrong turn.
A letter and a word. Every space gets one of each: A for the conference room, B for the library, C for the office.
Big on black. White type on black panels, readable from the far end of a corridor.
Out onto the street. The same signs, as sandwich boards and a hanging sign, bring people in from the pavement.
New members now find the café on their first day, and the sandwich boards double as a noticeboard for events.
The founders say the boiler room has been very quiet.
Dev Patel, community manager at The Yard

/projects/loudhouse-records.title: Loudhouse Records website and app
/projects/loudhouse-records.description: A website and listening app for an independent record label, built around big covers you flip through like a crate.
h2: A record shop in your pocket
h3: “The app feels like the shop on a good Saturday. Our staff use it behind the counter now.”
p: A website and listening app for an independent record label, designed to feel like flicking through a crate in a shop.
We designed the website and app around big, bold covers you flip through, with one-tap listening and a weekly pick from the people who run the label.

Loudhouse has been releasing records since the eighties and still runs a shop on the ground floor of its studio. They wanted the website and app to feel like the shop: a bit chaotic and very personal.
The old site was a list. Every record had the same small thumbnail and the same grey text, so the classics and the new releases looked identical.
We started by watching people in the shop.
Flip, don’t scroll. Covers fill the screen and you flip through them like a crate.
A person behind every pick. Each week someone at the label picks a record and writes two lines about it.
One tap to listen. Every cover plays a track the moment you open it.
People now spend twice as long on the site, and the weekly pick has become the label’s most-read email.
The shop staff use the app behind the counter too.

/projects/slow-burn-candles.title: Slow Burn Candles packaging
/projects/slow-burn-candles.description: Square, colour-coded gift boxes for a small-batch candle maker, built to stack into a shop window.
h3: “A shop built a whole window out of our boxes without being asked. That told me everything.”
p: Gift boxes for a candle maker whose candles take two days to set, so the boxes had to look worth the wait.
We gave every scent its own colour and a square box that stacks into a wall, with the candle sitting in a lilac tray inside.
Slow Burn’s candles are poured by hand and cure for two days before they are ready. The packaging was a plain white box with a sticker.
In a shop, white boxes disappear. The candles sold to people who already knew them, but nobody new was picking them up.
We designed for the shop window first.
A colour per hour. Morning is orange, dusk is lilac, midnight is green.
Built to stack. Square boxes, so a shop can build a whole wall of them in the window.
Open it twice. The lid lifts to show the candle in a tray, and the tray works as a dish afterwards.
The new boxes went into four shops in the first month.
One of them built a window out of nothing but orange boxes and sold out of the morning scent in a week.
Sam Reyes, founder of Slow Burn

/projects/bramble-flower-studio.title: Bramble Flower Studio identity
/projects/bramble-flower-studio.description: A colourful identity kit for a flower studio: an arched mark, four strong colours and stationery that mixes in any order.
h2: Wrapping as loud as the flowers
h3: “I can wrap an order from the kit in two minutes, and every one still looks like us.”
p: An identity for a flower studio that wraps its bouquets in more colour than most florists put in the flowers.
We built a palette of four strong colours, an arched mark taken from the shop window, and a kit of stickers, tags, envelopes, folders and bags that can be mixed in any order.
Bramble’s bouquets are known for their wrapping: three papers, a ribbon and a handwritten tag. The owner asked us to turn that habit into an identity.
Florist brands tend to go soft: pastel pink, a script font, a single rose. Bramble is none of those things, and the old cream stationery made her look like everyone else on the high street.
We designed a kit rather than a logo.
Four colours, no favourites. Orange, green, purple and pink, used in any combination.
An arch for a mark. The shape of the shop’s front window, simple enough to cut out of card.
Paper first. Every piece was mocked up in real paper on the studio table before we drew it on screen.
Every order now goes out in a different mix of the same kit: envelopes, tags, folders and bags.
No two look the same, and all of them look like Bramble.

/projects/larder-and-co.title: Larder & Co. packaging range
/projects/larder-and-co.description: How we turned a farm shop’s thirty own-label products into one bright, patterned packaging family.
h3: “We used to dread new products. Now a new tin is a day’s work and it already looks like it belongs.”
p: A packaging range for a farm shop’s own-label food, from tinned tomatoes to yoghurt, that looks like one family on the shelf.
We built one patterned system in bright colours, one colour per product family, so the range looks related from across the shop and each tin is easy to find.
Larder & Co. sells its own food next to local produce: tinned tomatoes, yoghurt cups, drinking yoghurt and granola. The food was great. The labels were all different.
Each product had been designed the week it launched, so the range looked like thirty small brands. Customers didn’t realise the yoghurt and the tomatoes came from the same kitchen.
We started with the shelf, not the logo.
Colour by family. Dairy is pink and purple, tins are green and orange, dry goods are kraft.
Patterns in clay. We pressed each pattern into plasticine and scanned it, so the lines wobble like they were made by hand.
One layout everywhere. Name, pattern and one line of copy, on a tin or on a yoghurt lid.
The range now reads as one family from across the shop, and a new product takes a day to design instead of a week.
The farm shop has since started selling its tins to other delis.
Priya Shah, co-owner of Larder & Co.

/projects/ethe-ceramics.title: Ethe Ceramics packaging and identity
/projects/ethe-ceramics.description: A round stamped label and kraft gift box for Ethe, a two-person pottery studio making stoneware mugs by hand.
h2: Let the clay do the talking
h3: “They understood the mugs should do the talking. The box only has to get them there in one piece, and it does.”
p: A quiet label and gift box for a pottery studio whose mugs are already loud enough on their own.
We left the mugs bare and put the brand on a small round stamped label and a kraft gift box that also does the shipping.
Ethe throws every mug by hand, and no two glazes come out the same. They asked us for a brand that would get out of the way.
Their first labels were big, glossy and printed in five colours. Next to a matte stoneware mug they looked like price tags.
We worked from the mug outwards.
Start with the glaze. We matched the label paper to the unglazed foot of the mug.
One round stamp. The mark is a circle with the name inside, small enough to sit on the side of a cup.
A box that does two jobs. The gift box is also the shipping box, so nothing gets thrown away on arrival.
The mugs now go out in a plain kraft box with a single round label, and the online shop sells out the way the market stall does.
We shot the product photos too, in the studio’s own window light.

/projects/musse-design-week.title: Musse Design Week identity
/projects/musse-design-week.description: How we built a stretchy red identity for a design festival, from flags and tees to a pocket-sized guidelines book.
h2: A festival with nothing but a name
h3: “Our volunteers made 300 pieces from the guidelines book and never once called the studio. That has never happened before.”
p: A loud red identity for a week-long design festival, built to work on a flag across the street and on a notebook in your hand.
We drew a stretchy wordmark that fills whatever it lands on, kept it to one red and one black, and printed it on flags, tees, notebooks and a guidelines book the volunteers actually read.

Musse brings together forty studios for one week every spring: open doors, talks and late shows. The organisers came to us four months before the first edition with a date, a list of venues and no visual identity at all.
A festival lives in a lot of places at once: flags on lampposts, lanyards, tote bags, a programme, a website. Most of it would be made by volunteers, in a hurry, on whatever printer was nearby.
We gave ourselves one rule: it has to survive a bad printer.
Clay first. We pressed the letters out of red plasticine to find a shape that still reads when it gets squashed.
One colour, one black. Red does the shouting; black holds the programme.
A book, not a PDF. The guidelines became a pocket book with every rule on one page.
The wordmark stretches to fill any shape, from a flag to a sticker, and the volunteers made over 300 pieces without asking us a single question.
That is the best review a design system can get.
Tom Okafor, festival director at Musse

/projects/fomo-collection-launch.title: Fomo streetwear launch campaign
/projects/fomo-collection-launch.description: A billboard, lightbox and launch-screen campaign for a streetwear drop that sold out in a weekend.
h2: Two days to make a city look up
h3: “One word and a date. I didn’t believe it would be enough until I saw the queue on Friday night.”
p: A launch campaign for a streetwear drop that only lasted two days, so every poster had to work in three seconds.
We built the campaign on one huge word and a date, then ran it on billboards, airport lightboxes, a subway wall and the screen at the launch party.

Fomo’s collections sell out fast, which is good news for the label and bad news for anyone who hears about them late. For the 21-07 drop they wanted a campaign people would see, remember and photograph within a single weekend.
A billboard gets about three seconds of attention, and the label had a lot to say: the date, the pieces, the pop-up address. Something had to give.
We cut the message down until it fitted on the side of a bus.
One word, one date. FOMO and 21-07, nothing else at first glance.
A soft glow. A blurred gradient that looks lit even on paper, so the posters and the lightboxes read as one campaign.
Test at walking pace. We stuck paper versions up on the studio stairs and asked people what they remembered on the way up.
The posters went up on Thursday and the queue started on Friday night.
The launch screen ran the same glow in motion, and the photos people took of the billboard did the rest.
Ana Ribeiro, head of brand at Fomo

/projects/nettle-and-bloom.title: Nettle & Bloom skincare identity
/projects/nettle-and-bloom.description: An identity, dark-glass packaging and printed lookbook for Nettle & Bloom, a herbal skincare brand grown in a walled garden.
h2: From the garden to the shelf
h3: “We wanted to look serious without losing the garden. The dark bottles did the first part, the pressed leaves did the second.”
p: An identity and packaging for a herbal skincare brand that grows half its ingredients in a walled garden.
We kept the bottles dark and plain with a small oval label, and let the lookbook, cards and envelopes carry the colour and the story.
Nettle & Bloom grows nettles, calendula and rosemary in a walled garden and turns them into oils and balms. The products sold well in local shops. The brand was a hand-drawn leaf.
Herbal brands all reach for the same things: green, a leaf, a script font. Nettle & Bloom needed to look like it knew what it was doing without losing the garden.
We split the job in two.
Quiet bottles. Dark glass and a small oval label, so the product looks serious on a bathroom shelf.
Loud paper. The lookbook, cards and envelopes carry the colour, the garden photos and the stories.
Pressed, not drawn. The leaf pattern is printed from real leaves pressed into clay.
The range launched online with a printed lookbook in every first order.
The hand cream still sells in threes.
Mia Chen, founder of Nettle & Bloom
